description_full: Worthington Enterprises, Inc. operates as an industrial manufacturing company. It operates through two segments, Consumer Products and Building Products. The Consumer Products segment provides products in the tools, outdoor living, and celebrations. Its products include hand-held torches, micro torches, lighters, accessories, and fuel for constructing, fixing making, and creating; precision and specialty hand, digital, and safety tools; drywall tools and accessories used for finishing and taping, cutting, siding, and roofing; propane-filled cylinders for torches, camping stoves and other applications, helium-filled balloon kits, and gas grills and pizza ovens. This segment sells its products primarily to mass merchandisers, retailers, and distributors under the Balloon Time, Bernzomatic, Coleman, Garden-Weasel, General, Halo, Hawkeye, Level5, Mag-Torch, Pactool International, and Worthington Pro Grade brand names. The Building Products segment provides pressurized containment solutions, such as refrigerant gas cylinders used in holding refrigerant gases for commercial, residential, and automotive air conditioning, and refrigeration systems; liquefied petroleum gas cylinders that holds fuel for residential and light commercial heating systems, barbeque grills and recreational vehicle equipment, industrial forklifts, and commercial/residential cooking; well water and expansion tanks used primarily in the residential and commercial markets; specialty products, including various fire suppression tanks, chemical tanks, and foam and adhesive tanks; and ceiling suspension systems and light gauge metal framing products. The company was formerly known as Worthington Industries, Inc. Worthington Enterprises, Inc. was founded in 1955 and is headquartered in Columbus, Ohio.

financial_summary: Worthington Enterprises, Inc. is a mid-cap industrials business with a $3.0B market cap on $1.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -35% over the past three years and -7% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 5% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 15% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $170M in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.45× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.1× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage of 12× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 37% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.69).

growth: Revenue has compounded at -34.5% over 3 years, -15.3% over 5 years and -6.9% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 28%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -2.4% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 4.0% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is -4, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
Analysts expect 12.0% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 37.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 54%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $6.7M sold).
It returns 2.7% a year to shareholders (1.5% in buybacks and 1.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, though it has been cut 7.0% a year over the last five.
